content.shloka:
Om Vishnur yonim kalpayatu, tvashtaa ruupaani pimshatu |
Aa sinchatu prajaapatir dhaaataa garbham dadhaatu te ||
content.meaning: May Lord Vishnu prepare the womb, may Tvashta shape the forms, may Prajapati sprinkle the seed, and may Dhata place the embryo in you.
content.transliteration:
Om Viṣṇur yoniṁ kalpayatu, Tvaṣṭā rūpāṇi piṁśatu |
Ā siñcatu Prajāpatir Dhātā garbhaṁ dadhātu te ||

content.shloka:
Dhaaataa dadhaatu daasakam tvishaa vivasvatah |
Tanme maa vishvato devaa devii savituh savitaa ||
content.meaning: May Dhata, the creator, bestow upon us ten-fold blessings by the radiance of Vivasvan. May all the divine forces and the creative energy of Savita bless us.
content.transliteration:
Dhātā dadhātu dāśakaṁ tviṣā Vivasvataḥ |
Tanme mā viśvato Devā Devī Savituḥ Savitā ||

content.shloka: The Garbhadhan Sanskar is the first of the sixteen Vedic sacraments (Shodash Sanskar). It is performed by the married couple with prayers for a righteous, healthy, and virtuous progeny. The couple observes purity of mind, body, and soul.
content.meaning: This sanskar sanctifies the act of conception and invokes divine blessings for a worthy child. Astrologically auspicious timings (muhurta) are chosen. The ritual includes offerings to Agni and chanting of Vedic mantras.
content.transliteration: The Garbhadhan Sanskar is the first of the sixteen Vedic sacraments (Shodash Sanskar). It is performed by the married couple with prayers for a righteous, healthy, and virtuous progeny. The couple observes purity of mind, body, and soul.

content.shloka:
Om Siniivaali prthu-shtroni yaa devi suprajaavatii |
Tasyaam me garbham aadhehi yah putro jagad-aayushah ||
content.meaning: O Goddess Sinivali, broad-hipped and bestower of good offspring, place in her a child who shall live a long and glorious life in this world.
content.transliteration:
Om Sinīvālī pṛthu-śṭroṇi yā Devī suprajāvatī |
Tasyāṁ me garbham ādhehi yaḥ putro jagad-āyuṣaḥ ||

content.shloka: Procedure: 1) Choose an auspicious day and muhurta. 2) Both husband and wife take a bath and wear clean garments. 3) Perform Ganapati puja and invoke Agni. 4) Chant the above mantras with offerings of ghee into the sacred fire. 5) Seek blessings from elders and Brahmins.
content.meaning: The ritual is performed with utmost devotion and purity. It emphasizes the spiritual dimension of parenthood and the desire for a child who will uphold Dharma.
content.transliteration: Procedure: 1) Choose an auspicious day and muhurta. 2) Both husband and wife take a bath and wear clean garments. 3) Perform Ganapati puja and invoke Agni. 4) Chant the above mantras with offerings of ghee into the sacred fire. 5) Seek blessings from elders and Brahmins.

content.shloka:
Om Pumaamsa-vaani janayatu pumaan sa yoniruta |
Pumaanso asau bhavantu ye prajaayante janaa iti ||
content.meaning: May male children be born to us, and may the womb yield heroic sons. May all offspring born to us be valiant and virtuous.
content.transliteration:
Om Pumāṁsāvānī janayatu pumān sa yoniruta |
Pumāṁso asau bhavantu ye prajāyante janā iti ||

content.shloka: The Punsavan Sanskar is performed in the second or third month of pregnancy. It is meant to ensure the healthy development of the child in the womb and to invoke divine protection over the mother and unborn child.
content.meaning: This ritual is one of the prenatal sacraments. The husband offers prayers and ghee into the fire while reciting Vedic mantras. A paste of banyan tree sap may be ritually applied.
content.transliteration: The Punsavan Sanskar is performed in the second or third month of pregnancy. It is meant to ensure the healthy development of the child in the womb and to invoke divine protection over the mother and unborn child.

content.shloka:
Om Suparnosi garutmaan trivrdya te shiro |
Gaayatram cha-akshuh stoma aatmaa saama te tanvam ||
content.meaning: O divine bird (Garuda), your three-fold head is the Trivrit hymn, Gayatri is your eye, Stoma is your soul, and Sama Veda is your body.
content.transliteration:
Om Suparṇosi Garutmān trivṛdya te śiro |
Gāyatraṁ cākṣuḥ stoma ātmā sāma te tanvam ||

content.shloka: Procedure: 1) Select an auspicious day in the 2nd or 3rd month of pregnancy. 2) Perform Ganapati Puja and Punyahavachan. 3) The husband sits beside the wife and chants Vedic mantras. 4) Offer ahutis (oblations) of ghee into the sacred fire. 5) Pray for the well-being of the mother and child.
content.meaning: The sanskar invokes the blessings of Lord Vishnu and other deities for a safe pregnancy and healthy offspring. It strengthens the spiritual bond between the parents and the unborn child.
content.transliteration: Procedure: 1) Select an auspicious day in the 2nd or 3rd month of pregnancy. 2) Perform Ganapati Puja and Punyahavachan. 3) The husband sits beside the wife and chants Vedic mantras. 4) Offer ahutis (oblations) of ghee into the sacred fire. 5) Pray for the well-being of the mother and child.

content.shloka:
Om Bhoor Bhuvah Svah | Tat Savitur Varenyam |
Bhargo Devasya Dheemahi | Dhiyo Yo Nah Prachodayaat ||
content.meaning: We meditate on the divine light of the Supreme Creator (Savita). May that radiant light illuminate our minds and inspire our intellect.
content.transliteration:
Om Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ | Tat Savitur Vareṇyam |
Bhargo Devasya Dhīmahi | Dhiyo Yo Naḥ Pracodayāt ||

content.shloka: The Simantonayan Sanskar (parting of the hair) is performed in the 4th, 6th, or 8th month of pregnancy. The husband parts the hair of the pregnant wife with a porcupine quill or a bunch of Darbha grass while chanting Vedic mantras.
content.meaning: This ceremony is meant to protect the pregnant woman from evil spirits and to bring joy and good fortune. It also fulfills the emotional needs of the expectant mother by showing her love and care.
content.transliteration: The Simantonayan Sanskar (parting of the hair) is performed in the 4th, 6th, or 8th month of pregnancy. The husband parts the hair of the pregnant wife with a porcupine quill or a bunch of Darbha grass while chanting Vedic mantras.

content.shloka:
Om Rekhaamah sushevaah sudughaah no asantu |
Bhadraah ritasya sadane siimanti ||
content.meaning: May the lines (of the hair parting) be auspicious, may they yield abundant blessings, and may the parting be sacred at the seat of cosmic order.
content.transliteration:
Om Rekhāmāḥ suśevāḥ sudughāḥ no asantu |
Bhadrāḥ ṛtasya sadane sīmantī ||

content.shloka: Procedure: 1) Choose a Shukla Paksha day. 2) Perform Ganapati puja. 3) The husband parts the wife's hair from front to back using a porcupine quill, Darbha grass, or Udumbara branch. 4) Chant the Simantonayan mantras. 5) Women sing auspicious songs and bless the expectant mother.
content.meaning: The ceremony creates a positive atmosphere for the mother-to-be. It is a celebration of impending motherhood and ensures the mental peace of the pregnant woman through communal blessings.
content.transliteration: Procedure: 1) Choose a Shukla Paksha day. 2) Perform Ganapati puja. 3) The husband parts the wife's hair from front to back using a porcupine quill, Darbha grass, or Udumbara branch. 4) Chant the Simantonayan mantras. 5) Women sing auspicious songs and bless the expectant mother.

content.shloka:
Om Aayushte vishvato mukham praanoyushte vishvatah |
Chakshuroshte vishvato-mukham shrotraushte vishvato-mukham ||
content.meaning: May you have long life facing all directions, may your breath of life face all directions, may your sight and hearing face all directions — may you be blessed with full vitality.
content.transliteration:
Om Āyuṣṭe viśvato mukham prāṇoyuṣṭe viśvataḥ |
Cakṣuroṣṭe viśvato-mukham śrotroṣṭe viśvato-mukham ||

content.shloka: Jatakarma Sanskar is the birth ceremony performed immediately after the child is born, before the umbilical cord is cut. The father touches the newborn and whispers Vedic mantras in the child's ear.
content.meaning: This is one of the most important Sanskars as it welcomes the newborn into the world with divine blessings. It establishes the first spiritual connection between the father and the child.
content.transliteration: Jatakarma Sanskar is the birth ceremony performed immediately after the child is born, before the umbilical cord is cut. The father touches the newborn and whispers Vedic mantras in the child's ear.

content.shloka:
Om Medhaam te devah savitaa medhaam devii sarasvatii |
Medhaam te ashvinau devau aadhaattaam pushkarasrajau ||
content.meaning: May God Savita bestow intelligence upon you, may Goddess Sarasvati grant you wisdom, and may the twin Ashvini Kumaras, adorned with lotus garlands, bless you with intellect.
content.transliteration:
Om Medhāṁ te Devaḥ Savitā medhāṁ Devī Sarasvatī |
Medhāṁ te Aśvinau Devau ādhāttāṁ puṣkarasrajau ||

content.shloka: Procedure: 1) The father performs the ritual immediately after birth. 2) He touches honey and ghee to the baby's lips with a gold spoon while chanting mantras. 3) He whispers the Gayatri mantra and the child's Gotra name in the right ear. 4) The mother then feeds the child for the first time. 5) Prayers are offered for the child's long life and wisdom.
content.meaning: The ritual of Jatakarma welcomes the newborn soul into the family lineage and invokes divine protection. The honey and ghee symbolize sweetness of speech and sharpness of intellect.
content.transliteration: Procedure: 1) The father performs the ritual immediately after birth. 2) He touches honey and ghee to the baby's lips with a gold spoon while chanting mantras. 3) He whispers the Gayatri mantra and the child's Gotra name in the right ear. 4) The mother then feeds the child for the first time. 5) Prayers are offered for the child's long life and wisdom.

content.shloka:
Om Vede te naama paramam guhaayaam | Vede te naama prithivyaam yat te |
Vede te naama dhenvaam antar aarabhya | Vede te naama vivasvat prathamajaayaam ||
content.meaning: I know your highest name hidden in the secret cave of the heart, I know your name on this earth, I know your name within the cow, and I know your name as the first-born of Vivasvan (the Sun).
content.transliteration:
Om Vede te nāma paramaṁ guhāyāṁ | Vede te nāma pṛthivyāṁ yat te |
Vede te nāma dhenvāṁ antar ārabhya | Vede te nāma Vivasvat prathamajāyāṁ ||

content.shloka:
Om Naamakarma karishyaami sumauhurte shubhe dine |
Aayushyam shree-karanam cha yashasvi parikirtitam ||
content.meaning: I shall perform the naming ceremony at an auspicious moment on a blessed day. May the name grant long life, prosperity, and fame to the child.
content.transliteration:
Om Nāmakarma kariṣyāmi sumuhūrte śubhe dine |
Āyuṣyaṁ śrīkaraṇaṁ ca yaśasvī parikīrtitam ||

content.shloka: Namkaran is the naming ceremony performed on the 11th or 12th day after birth, or on any auspicious day thereafter. The child is given a formal name based on the Nakshatra (birth star), family tradition, and the name of a deity.
content.meaning: The name shapes the child's identity and destiny. According to Vedic tradition, the name should have an even number of syllables and start with the syllable associated with the birth Nakshatra.
content.transliteration: Namkaran is the naming ceremony performed on the 11th or 12th day after birth, or on any auspicious day thereafter. The child is given a formal name based on the Nakshatra (birth star), family tradition, and the name of a deity.

content.shloka:
Om Aham asmi prathamajaa ritaasya |
Poorvam devebhya amritasya naabhai |
Yo maa dadaati sa id eva maa avah ||
content.meaning: I am the first-born of the cosmic order. Before the gods, I am the center of immortality. He who gives to me, truly he protects me.
content.transliteration:
Om Aham asmi prathamajā ṛtāsya |
Pūrvaṁ devebhya amṛtasya nābhai |
Yo mā dadāti sa id eva mā avaḥ ||

content.shloka: Procedure: 1) On the chosen day, bathe the child and dress in new clothes. 2) Perform Ganapati puja and Havan. 3) The father or priest writes the chosen name on a plate of rice using a gold stick. 4) The father whispers the name in the child's right ear three times. 5) Elders bless the child and distribute sweets.
content.meaning: The Namkaran ceremony formally introduces the child to the family, community, and the divine. It is a joyous occasion accompanied by prayers, feasting, and the blessings of all present.
content.transliteration: Procedure: 1) On the chosen day, bathe the child and dress in new clothes. 2) Perform Ganapati puja and Havan. 3) The father or priest writes the chosen name on a plate of rice using a gold stick. 4) The father whispers the name in the child's right ear three times. 5) Elders bless the child and distribute sweets.

content.shloka:
Om Annapaate annasya no dehi anamiivasya shusminah |
Pra praadaataaraam taarisha oorjam no dhehi dvipade chatushpade ||
content.meaning: O Lord of food, grant us food that is free from disease and full of vitality. Nourish the giver, and grant strength to all beings — two-footed and four-footed alike.
content.transliteration:
Om Annapāte annasya no dehi anāmīvasya śuṣmiṇaḥ |
Pra prādātāraṁ tāriṣa ūrjaṁ no dhehi dvipade catuṣpade ||

content.shloka: Annaprashan is the first feeding ceremony, performed when the child is 6 months old (for boys) or 5 months old (for girls). The child is given solid food (usually kheer or rice pudding) for the first time.
content.meaning: This sanskar marks the transition from liquid to solid food. It is believed to strengthen the child's body and mind. The ceremony thanks the divine for sustaining the child and prays for continued nourishment.
content.transliteration: Annaprashan is the first feeding ceremony, performed when the child is 6 months old (for boys) or 5 months old (for girls). The child is given solid food (usually kheer or rice pudding) for the first time.

content.shloka:
Om Shaanno deveer abhishtaya aapo bhavantu peetaye |
Sham yor abhisravantu nah ||
content.meaning: May the divine waters be for our well-being and nourishment. May they flow towards us with blessings and peace.
content.transliteration:
Om Śānno Devīr abhiṣṭaya āpo bhavantu pītaye |
Śam yor abhisravantu naḥ ||

content.shloka: Procedure: 1) Choose an auspicious day and muhurta. 2) Bathe and dress the child in new clothes. 3) Perform Ganapati puja and invoke Annapurna Devi. 4) The maternal uncle or the father feeds the child the first morsel of food (payasam/kheer). 5) Various items (books, clay, gold, food) are placed before the child to predict future inclination.
content.meaning: The ceremony is a celebration of growth and health. The items placed before the child represent knowledge, wealth, and sustenance — whichever the child reaches for first is said to indicate their future path.
content.transliteration: Procedure: 1) Choose an auspicious day and muhurta. 2) Bathe and dress the child in new clothes. 3) Perform Ganapati puja and invoke Annapurna Devi. 4) The maternal uncle or the father feeds the child the first morsel of food (payasam/kheer). 5) Various items (books, clay, gold, food) are placed before the child to predict future inclination.

content.shloka:
Om Yena pootah puurve tasmaat |
Kshurena savitaa tvachah |
Sha indra varunah sha brihaspatiraghaashamsah ||
content.meaning: With the razor by which Savita purified the ancestors, may Indra, Varuna, and Brihaspati cleanse and protect this child from all evil.
content.transliteration:
Om Yena pūtaḥ pūrve tasmāt |
Kṣureṇa Savitā tvacaḥ |
Śa Indra Varuṇaḥ śa Bṛhaspatiraghāśaṁsaḥ ||

content.shloka: Mundan (Chudakarana) Sanskar is the first head-shaving ceremony of the child, performed in the 1st or 3rd year. The hair that was present at birth is considered impure and is shaved off to promote the healthy growth of new hair.
content.meaning: This ceremony symbolizes purification and the removal of past-life residues. It is often performed at a holy pilgrimage site. The shaved hair is offered to a sacred river or deity.
content.transliteration: Mundan (Chudakarana) Sanskar is the first head-shaving ceremony of the child, performed in the 1st or 3rd year. The hair that was present at birth is considered impure and is shaved off to promote the healthy growth of new hair.

content.shloka:
Om Aayur-daa agne harasaa srutasya |
Tvag-astu sahasraposhaaya varchase ||
content.meaning: O Fire God (Agni), grant long life with your radiance. May the skin (and new hair) grow for a thousand-fold nourishment and brilliance.
content.transliteration:
Om Āyur-dā Agne harasā sṛtasya |
Tvag-astu sahasrapoṣāya varcase ||

content.shloka: Procedure: 1) Choose an auspicious day (often at a tirtha like Tirupati, Varanasi, or Pandharpur). 2) Perform Ganapati puja and Havan. 3) The barber shaves the child's head while mantras are chanted. 4) Apply sandalwood paste and turmeric on the head. 5) The shaved hair is immersed in a sacred river. 6) Feed Brahmins and distribute prasad.
content.meaning: Mundan is one of the most widely observed Sanskars across Hindu traditions. It purifies the child, promotes health, and is often the child's first visit to a holy place.
content.transliteration: Procedure: 1) Choose an auspicious day (often at a tirtha like Tirupati, Varanasi, or Pandharpur). 2) Perform Ganapati puja and Havan. 3) The barber shaves the child's head while mantras are chanted. 4) Apply sandalwood paste and turmeric on the head. 5) The shaved hair is immersed in a sacred river. 6) Feed Brahmins and distribute prasad.

content.shloka:
Om Yajnopaviitam paramam pavitram prjaapater yat sahajam purastaad |
Aayushyam agryam pratimuncha shubhram yajnopaviitam balam astu tejah ||
content.meaning: The sacred thread (Yajnopavita) is supremely holy, born with Prajapati from the beginning. Wearing it grants long life, purity, strength, and radiance.
content.transliteration:
Om Yajñopavītam paramaṁ pavitraṁ Prajāpater yat sahajaṁ purastāt |
Āyuṣyam agryaṁ pratimunca śubhraṁ yajñopavītaṁ balam astu tejaḥ ||

content.shloka: The Upanayan Sanskar is the sacred thread ceremony that marks the beginning of formal Vedic education. The child becomes a 'Dvija' (twice-born) and is initiated into the Gayatri Mantra by the Guru (teacher).
content.meaning: This sanskar is traditionally performed at age 8 for Brahmins, 11 for Kshatriyas, and 12 for Vaishyas. It is one of the most significant rites of passage in Hindu life.
content.transliteration: The Upanayan Sanskar is the sacred thread ceremony that marks the beginning of formal Vedic education. The child becomes a 'Dvija' (twice-born) and is initiated into the Gayatri Mantra by the Guru (teacher).

content.shloka:
Om Bhoor Bhuvah Svah | Tat Savitur Varenyam |
Bhargo Devasya Dheemahi | Dhiyo Yo Nah Prachodayaat ||
content.meaning: We meditate on the glorious light of the divine Savita. May that supreme light illuminate our intellect and guide us on the path of righteousness.
content.transliteration:
Om Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ | Tat Savitur Vareṇyam |
Bhargo Devasya Dhīmahi | Dhiyo Yo Naḥ Pracodayāt ||

content.shloka:
Om Medhaavii tejasvi bhuyaasam | Aham vrikshasya rerivaa |
Kiirtih prishtham iva ucchaih rashi shraih braahmanena praaptam ||
content.meaning: May I become wise and radiant. Like a tree, may my fame rise high. May I attain the summit of Brahmanical knowledge and glory.
content.transliteration:
Om Medhāvī tejasvī bhūyāsam | Ahaṁ vṛkṣasya rerivā |
Kīrtiḥ pṛṣṭham iva uccaiḥ rāśi śraiḥ brāhmaṇena prāptam ||

content.shloka: Procedure: 1) The boy is bathed and dressed in new clothes. 2) Havan is performed. 3) The Acharya (Guru) places the sacred thread (Yajnopavita) over the left shoulder. 4) The Guru whispers the Gayatri Mantra in the boy's right ear. 5) The boy begins his first bhiksha (alms-seeking) from his mother. 6) He vows to observe Brahmacharya (celibacy and discipline) during his student years.
content.meaning: Upanayan literally means 'bringing near' — the child is brought near to the Guru and to sacred knowledge. The three threads represent the three debts — to the Gods, ancestors, and sages.
content.transliteration: Procedure: 1) The boy is bathed and dressed in new clothes. 2) Havan is performed. 3) The Acharya (Guru) places the sacred thread (Yajnopavita) over the left shoulder. 4) The Guru whispers the Gayatri Mantra in the boy's right ear. 5) The boy begins his first bhiksha (alms-seeking) from his mother. 6) He vows to observe Brahmacharya (celibacy and discipline) during his student years.

content.shloka:
Om Brahmachaarinee aagat samidhaah samidhya aagneh |
Agner aayurdadhaatu brhaspatiragne aayurdadhaatu ||
content.meaning: The Brahmachari has come with sacred fuel. May Agni grant him long life, and may Brihaspati, through Agni, bestow longevity.
content.transliteration:
Om Brahmacāriṇī āgat samidhāḥ samidhya Āgneḥ |
Agner āyurdadhātu Bṛhaspatiragne āyurdadhātu ||

content.shloka:
Om Dharmecha arthecha kaamecha naati-charaami |
Dharmecha arthecha kaamecha naati-charaamah ||
content.meaning: In matters of Dharma, Artha (prosperity), and Kama (desire), I shall not transgress. We shall not transgress the boundaries of righteousness in these three pursuits.
content.transliteration:
Om Dharmeća artheća kāmeća nāti-carāmi |
Dharmeća artheća kāmeća nāti-carāmaḥ ||

content.shloka: Vivah (marriage) is the most elaborate and significant of all Sanskars. It unites two individuals in a sacred bond witnessed by Agni (fire), family, and the divine. The ceremony involves multiple rituals spanning several hours.
content.meaning: Hindu marriage is not merely a social contract but a spiritual sacrament. The couple vows to walk together through the four aims of life — Dharma, Artha, Kama, and Moksha.
content.transliteration: Vivah (marriage) is the most elaborate and significant of all Sanskars. It unites two individuals in a sacred bond witnessed by Agni (fire), family, and the divine. The ceremony involves multiple rituals spanning several hours.

content.shloka:
Saptapadi — Idam Vishnur-vichakrame tredha nidadhe padam |
Samoolham asya paamsure ||
content.meaning: Saptapadi (Seven Steps): Like Vishnu who strode across the universe in three steps, let us take seven steps together. The entire world is established in His dust.
content.transliteration:
Saptapadī — Idaṁ Viṣṇur-vicakrame tredhā nidadhe padam |
Samūlham asya pāṁsure ||

content.shloka: The Seven Vows (Saptapadi): Step 1 — For nourishment. Step 2 — For strength and vitality. Step 3 — For prosperity and wealth. Step 4 — For happiness and harmony. Step 5 — For progeny. Step 6 — For long life together. Step 7 — For eternal friendship and companionship.
content.meaning: With each step around the sacred fire, the couple makes a vow for their life together. After the seventh step, the bond becomes irrevocable. They become lifelong partners in dharma.
content.transliteration: The Seven Vows (Saptapadi): Step 1 — For nourishment. Step 2 — For strength and vitality. Step 3 — For prosperity and wealth. Step 4 — For happiness and harmony. Step 5 — For progeny. Step 6 — For long life together. Step 7 — For eternal friendship and companionship.

content.shloka:
Om Grihnami te saubhagatvaaya hastam |
Mayaa patyaa jaradastir yatha asah |
Bhago aryamaa savitaa purandhir |
Mahyam tvaam aadur gaarhapatyaya devaah ||
content.meaning: I hold your hand for good fortune, so that with me as your husband you may grow old. Bhaga, Aryama, Savita, and Purandhi — the gods have given you to me for the household fire.
content.transliteration:
Om Gṛhṇāmi te saubhagatvāya hastam |
Mayā patyā jaradastir yathā asaḥ |
Bhago Aryamā Savitā Purandhir |
Mahyaṁ tvām ādur gārhapatyāya devāḥ ||

content.shloka: Procedure: 1) Varapuja (welcoming the groom). 2) Kanyadan (giving away the bride). 3) Vivah Homa (sacred fire ritual). 4) Paanigrahan (holding hands). 5) Laja Homa (offering of puffed rice). 6) Saptapadi (seven steps). 7) Sindoor Daan and Mangalsutra. 8) Ashirvad (blessings from elders).
content.meaning: Each step of the Vivah ceremony carries deep spiritual significance. The sacred fire (Agni) serves as the eternal witness. The rituals ensure divine blessings for the couple's journey ahead.
content.transliteration: Procedure: 1) Varapuja (welcoming the groom). 2) Kanyadan (giving away the bride). 3) Vivah Homa (sacred fire ritual). 4) Paanigrahan (holding hands). 5) Laja Homa (offering of puffed rice). 6) Saptapadi (seven steps). 7) Sindoor Daan and Mangalsutra. 8) Ashirvad (blessings from elders).

content.shloka:
Om Asato maa sadgamaya | Tamaso maa jyotirgamaya |
Mrityor maa amritam gamaya ||
content.meaning: Lead me from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to immortality.
content.transliteration:
Om Asato mā sadgamaya | Tamaso mā jyotirgamaya |
Mṛtyor mā amṛtaṁ gamaya ||

content.shloka: Antyeshti (last sacrifice) is the final Sanskar, performed after death. The body is cremated on a funeral pyre while Vedic mantras are chanted. It is the soul's final rite of passage from this world.
content.meaning: Hindu belief holds that the body is made of five elements (Pancha Bhuta) and must be returned to them. Cremation releases the soul (Atman) from the physical body so it can continue its journey.
content.transliteration: Antyeshti (last sacrifice) is the final Sanskar, performed after death. The body is cremated on a funeral pyre while Vedic mantras are chanted. It is the soul's final rite of passage from this world.

content.shloka:
Om Vaisvaanaraaya preetaye svaahaa |
Sooryaaya svaahaaa | Mrityave svaahaaa ||
content.meaning: Oblations to Vaishvanara (Universal Fire), svaha! To Surya (the Sun God), svaha! To Mrityu (Death), svaha!
content.transliteration:
Om Vaiśvānarāya prītaye svāhā |
Sūryāya svāhā | Mṛtyave svāhā ||

content.shloka:
Om Nainam chhindanti shastraani nainam dahati paavakah |
Na chainam kledayantyaapo na shoshayati maarutah ||
content.meaning: The soul cannot be cut by weapons, nor burned by fire, nor dissolved by water, nor dried by the wind. (Bhagavad Gita 2.23)
content.transliteration:
Om Nainaṁ chindanti śastrāṇi nainaṁ dahati pāvakaḥ |
Na cainaṁ kledayantyāpo na śoṣayati mārutaḥ ||

content.shloka: Procedure: 1) The body is bathed and wrapped in white cloth. 2) It is placed on the funeral pyre with feet facing south. 3) The eldest son (or chief mourner) lights the pyre while chanting mantras. 4) Ghee and sandalwood are offered to the fire. 5) After cremation, the ashes are collected on the 3rd day and immersed in a holy river. 6) Shraddha (memorial) rituals are performed on the 13th day.
content.meaning: The Antyeshti Sanskar ensures a peaceful departure of the soul. The 13-day mourning period allows the family to grieve while performing rituals that aid the soul's onward journey.
content.transliteration: Procedure: 1) The body is bathed and wrapped in white cloth. 2) It is placed on the funeral pyre with feet facing south. 3) The eldest son (or chief mourner) lights the pyre while chanting mantras. 4) Ghee and sandalwood are offered to the fire. 5) After cremation, the ashes are collected on the 3rd day and immersed in a holy river. 6) Shraddha (memorial) rituals are performed on the 13th day.

content.shloka:
Om Tryambakam yajaamahe sugandhim pushti-vardhanam |
Urvaarukam iva bandhanaan mrityor muksheeya maamritaat ||
content.meaning: We worship the three-eyed Lord (Shiva) who is fragrant and nourishes all. May He liberate us from death, just as a cucumber is severed from its vine — grant us immortality.
content.transliteration:
Om Tryambakaṁ yajāmahe sugandhiṁ puṣṭi-vardhanam |
Urvārukam iva bandhanān mṛtyor mukṣīya māmṛtāt ||
